semantic_correction.stem: A nonpregnant adult client who smokes cigarettes wants to quit. Which nursing teaching is most consistent with current CDC guidance?

options.A: Use behavioral counseling together with an appropriate smoking-cessation medication when clinically suitable, and arrange follow-up support as the quit attempt continues.
options.B: Begin with counseling alone and postpone cessation medication until several unsupported quit attempts have failed, even when medication is otherwise appropriate.
options.C: Use cessation medication as the main treatment and omit counseling and follow-up unless withdrawal symptoms remain severe after the medication is started.
options.D: Give brief advice to quit and wait for the client to request more help later, rather than offering counseling, medication, and planned follow-up now.

semantic_correction.rationale: A is correct. Current CDC guidance for nonpregnant adults states that behavioral counseling and smoking-cessation medication are each effective and are more effective when used together. CDC advises clinicians to offer a combination of counseling and medications and to follow patients over time because quitting may require repeated attempts and ongoing support. B is incorrect because CDC does not require multiple failed unaided attempts before offering appropriate medication with counseling. C is incorrect because medication does not replace behavioral counseling, and follow-up remains an important component of treatment. D is incorrect because brief advice can help, but current CDC clinical guidance goes further by recommending active treatment, referral to additional support when useful, and follow-up rather than waiting passively for the client to return after difficulty or relapse.
semantic_correction.educational_objective: Teach nonpregnant adults who smoke that combining behavioral counseling with clinically appropriate cessation medication and planned follow-up provides stronger evidence-based support for quitting than either treatment alone or brief advice without ongoing assistance.
semantic_correction.source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
semantic_correction.source_document_title: How to Quit Smoking; Clinical Interventions to Treat Tobacco Use and Dependence Among Adults
semantic_correction.source_version_date: How to Quit Smoking dated May 15, 2024; Clinical Interventions dated May 14, 2024; current CDC pages accessed August 21, 2026
semantic_correction.source_locator: How to Quit Smoking → What to know and 'Counseling plus medications': counseling and medication together give people who smoke the best chance of quitting; 'Get help quitting today': a health care professional can help select treatment and connect the client with resources. Clinical Interventions to Treat Tobacco Use and Dependence Among Adults → 'For non-pregnant patients' → Behavioral counseling, Medication, and Combining treatments: counseling and medication are each effective and are more effective together; 'Offer patients treatment': offer a combination of counseling and medications; 'Follow up with patients': assess progress over time, provide additional support, and recognize that several quit attempts may be needed.
semantic_correction.source_claim_supported: For nonpregnant adults who smoke, CDC supports combining behavioral counseling with appropriate cessation medication and providing follow-up support rather than relying on either treatment alone or a single unsupported encounter.

audit_findings_append.finding: The revised item tests combined counseling, clinically appropriate cessation medication, and follow-up for a nonpregnant adult with one clearly best answer and no conspicuous absolute-word cue.

option_audit.A: Correct. CDC directly supports combined counseling and medication for nonpregnant adults and recommends follow-up over time.
option_audit.B: Incorrect. CDC does not require repeated unsupported quit failures before offering appropriate evidence-based pharmacotherapy with counseling.
option_audit.C: Incorrect. It incorrectly substitutes medication for counseling and makes follow-up conditional rather than routine supportive care.
option_audit.D: Incorrect. Brief advice can help, but CDC recommends active treatment and follow-up rather than waiting for the client to seek more help later.

ambiguity_check: No second defensible answer. A alone combines the CDC-supported treatment modalities with follow-up; B unnecessarily delays medication, C omits counseling and routine follow-up, and D stops at brief advice without offering the recommended treatment package.
cueing_check: All four choices are parallel cessation-management plans of comparable length and specificity; the prior 'always' and 'only' distractor cues were removed, and A is not uniquely privileged by formatting or detail.
